messages.subject: Comparing densities from different areas
parts:
Dear member's list,

I'm using for the first time the Distance software and I have some questions
about comparing my results from each area (3) First, it was decide to treat
the different areas seperately because the main objective of this study is
to see the diferenciation of occupancy among two species in those areas
(guanacos,huemules) also the visibility aren't the same due to different
vegetation and also because a post-stratification by cluster size seems
accurate in the case of the guanacos. I'm now trying to establish if my
datas are distributed normally in each areas and then do a statistic
analysis (ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis) to see if there's a significant
difference among the areas for each specie. To see if the distribution of my
datas is normal, I was thinking to use the density (D= N/2wL) for each
transect and then compare them...is it a better way to do it?

During this study we also collect information about the number of faeces of
foxes in the areas. Since we don't have the decay rate and the number of
faeces produced daily by foxes, I think the only information I can use is
the index of faeces by kilometer of transect. I don't think I can use
Distance's software since we don't have the perpendicular Distance either
(the faeces were on the line). Is there an other option? And if not, can we
compare this index among the transects to see if the datas are distributed
normally?(like the datas collected for the guanacos and huemules)

Many thanks,

Julie Langevin
Student in international ecology of the University of Sherbrooke, Canada

messages.author: 12f269733c6eb9a2
messages.subject: Re: Comparing densities from different areas
parts:
Julie:

There are several problems with your approach. Unless you have an
immense number of transects (>30) you won't be able to establish the
normality (or lack thereof) of the estimates produced from each. And I
don't think there is a reason to determine the normality of that
distribution.

Your transects are not independent replicates because you are using the
same detection function for each transect within one of your areas.
Because they share the same detection function (or f-hat(0) if you
wish), they will have a covariance between them, so you ought not use
them as replicates.

You would be better served to use an analysis method described in
Buckland, S.T., Russell, R.E., Dickson, B.G., Saab, V.A., Gorman, D.G.
and Block, W.M. 2009. Analysing designed experiments in distance
sampling. Journal of Agricultural, Biological and Environmental
Statistics 14, 432-442.
<http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/stb/buckland%20et%20al%20jabes%202009.pdf>
http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/stb/buckland%20et%20al%20jabes%202009.pdf

Regarding the faeces analysis, you indeed cannot use distance sampling
if there are no measured distances. You will have count data unadjusted
for detectability so you will have to rely upon the untestable
assumption that detectability is unchanging among your study areas.
That is a much more unlikely assumption than anything you might want to
demonstrate regarding normality.
